git add src/money.js && git commit -m "Fix floating-point precision in price parsing

Use Math.round() after multiplying by 100 to handle floating-point
precision errors. Prices like 39.95 would convert to 3995.0000000000005
instead of 3995, causing validation to fail.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Haiku 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>"

claude.result: Done! The fix now applies `Math.round()` to both `parseEuros()` and `cellCents()` functions in `src/money.js`, plus to the `decimalCommaToCents()` call to handle European decimal comma format too. This ensures that floating-point precision errors (like 39.95 * 100 = 3995.0000000000005) are properly rounded to whole cents. All 50 tests pass, and you can now add your Gym membership at €39.95.
step_results:
Done! The issue was a floating-point precision bug in the `parseEuros()` and `cellCents()` functions in `src/money.js`. When 39.95 is multiplied by 100 to convert to cents, JavaScript's floating-point arithmetic produces 3995.0000000000005 instead of exactly 3995, causing the validation to reject it as a non-integer.

The fix adds `Math.round()` after the multiplication to properly round to the nearest whole number. This is the standard approach for handling currency conversions. Both 39.95 and your other prices (12.99, 10.99) now work correctly. All 50 existing tests pass with the fix.
